Entertainment.title: Music streaming: Why we're listening to so many old songs
Entertainment.text:
More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.

The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.

Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.

This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.

In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.

So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?

In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.

Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs, external were released 12 months ago, or earlier.

The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.

It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".

It's a similar story in the US.

There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, external, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.

Likewise, in America, Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas has become the longest-running number one in US chart history.

The reality, of course, is that hits need to achieve "millions of streams a day, external" to reach the top of the charts.

But according to the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, nearly two thirds of streams are of music recorded by "only the top 0.4% of artists, external".

As we increasingly cling on to our favourites, aspiring artists may be suffering.

Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song.

"It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard, external.

"For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?"

It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.

Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation.

"You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News.

"Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."

Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.

This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.

Chiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.

Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.

Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.

To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced.

"Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."

When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies, external against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.

New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.

Entertainment.title: Sam Fender calls out ticket prices ahead of 2027 tour sale
Entertainment.text:
Sam Fender has said he has removed a ticket category from sale after being unhappy with pricing for his upcoming tour.

The 32-year-old announced his Proper Massive Stadium Tour earlier this week, which will visit Newcastle, Cardiff, London, Edinburgh, Dublin and Manchester in summer 2027.

While tickets are yet to go on sale, Fender responded to a post on social media which claimed to outline the expected ticket prices.

The Geordie musician now appears to have lowered the prices and said the "costs are astronomical compared to two years ago" but he could not control the venue or ticketing fees.

Tickets are due to go on general sale at 09:30 GMT on Friday, with a pre-sale at the same time on Wednesday.

Fender initially said he was "not happy" with the reported prices.

"They're getting changed," he said on Instagram.

"It got inflated well more than I'd had in mind, it should only be inflated in relation to the cost of putting the show on."

Entertainment.title: Jazzy: The Irish DJ dropping her debut after a billion streams
Entertainment.text:
Releasing your first album is a big step for any artist, but for Jazzy it's one that's followed some huge strides.

The Irish singer and DJ has been streamed more than a billion times and worked with industry heavyweights including Calvin Harris.

If that's not enough, on Saturday she has her biggest gig yet when she'll be playing tracks like No Bad Vibes and Someday in front of a home crowd in Dublin.

For Jazzy, writing an album has always been in the back of her mind and now, finally, it's time to hit send.

She's previously released dozens of singles, building up a monthly listenership over 10 million strong, but Peace and Patience is her first full-length work.

"It's been quite a few years of creating some smaller projects," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"That's given me enough experience now to feel like it was the right moment."

The 30-year-old, real name Yasmine Byrne, has been putting out music for more than five years and collabed with the likes of Sonny Fodera, Rossi. and KILIMANJARO on some of her biggest tracks.

Dance music has boomed in recent years, with Spotify previously telling Newsbeat that since 2020 the amount under-25s listen to the genre has grown by more than 73% globally.

It also dominated festival line-ups over the summer - including Radio 1's Big Weekend which dedicated all its stages to dance music on the opening night.

But artists in the genre have often moved away from albums, opting instead to release EPs and singles.

Jazzy has noticed the change, saying it feels "a lot different now, with people kind of siding with virality rather than quality of music".

"When I was making the album, I wasn't thinking about going viral or anything like that. I just wanted to make something that was true to me and sounded like a Jazzy album.

"I like to let things happen quite organically and I try to just let the music speak to me."

Jazzy is rooted in the Dublin club scene, starting her career as part of a group called Powerful Creative Minds in the city.

But as more and more clubs close, the DJ says there are fewer opportunities for artists to cut their teeth offline.

"When I first started going out, there was a lot more going on," she says.

"There was a lot more nightclubs to go to and it's very different when we look at it now, which is sad.

"There's definitely a home for dance music on the internet of course but club culture is very important and I think that's something that we need to keep going for sure."

Latest figures from the Night Time Industries Association, external suggest about 12 venues are closing across the UK every month, with almost 30% of the night time economy lost since the coronavirus pandemic.

"I hope to God that it doesn't disappear, the club scene altogether," says Jazzy, who describes a similar issue in Ireland.

"We all need to try and put a hand in to keep it going."

Jazzy's taking her new album on tour across the UK from next month, but first she has her biggest gig yet: Dublin's 3Arena in front of a home crowd.

Even after a Coachella set and supporting Calvin Harris, she describes this as the "biggest milestone of my career to date".

While she says fans can mostly expect her brand of uplifting records on the album, she says it's also more personal than her usual work.

She highlights one track in particular, Invisible, as a change from her more upbeat releases. It deals with a bad experience she had in the music industry, describing it as "like my first ever diss track".

"I hope [fans] learn a little bit more about me, because that was one of my goals with the album - to open up a little bit about experiences in life as well.

"So there's a little message from me in each song."

Entertainment.title: Milton Keynes: Why these four people think it's UK City of Culture
Entertainment.text:
Milton Keynes has often been dismissed as somewhere not worth pulling off the M1 for, frequently by people who have no plans on visiting in the first place. But recently, that tide has turned. The BBC spoke to four people who have been part of the city's evolution and believe it has a chance of being crowned the UK City of Culture for 2029.

In 2025, the city was named one of the best places to live and work in the UK.

It is now in with a real chance of winning the £10m prize having been shortlisted as one of four places for the City of Culture contest.

The shorthand used to describe Milton Keynes often refers to concrete cows and its many roundabouts.

However, for Irish-born Nigerian creative Maureen Onwunali, who grew up and lives here, the city has so much more to offer.

While researching for her poem as part of the city's original bid, she said she found it "surprisingly so fascinating".

"I devoured all of these facts so now at any party, I have at least five Milton Keynes facts."

In "An ode to Milton Keynes", Onwunali refers to "the colossus, the world's first programmable computer" and "self-driving cars on Roman roads".

She told the BBC: "It's so funny because I tell people about Milton Keynes and culture and they look at me as if I'm being sarcastic, because Milton Keynes has this stereotype of being soulless.

"But there's so many artists who've come out of Milton Keynes.

"A lot do go off to bigger cities like London or Manchester but I think it's just a matter of harnessing their talents and having opportunities to platform them."

Cultural events already held in the city include Reggae Land at the National Bowl and the Milton Keynes International Festival. This is alongside annual functions held at Campbell Park such as Art in the Park, the Zimbabwe Heritage Festival, MK Pride and Oktoberfest.

On the day the shortlist was announced, a four-month exhibition celebrating the life of British artist Laurence Stephen Lowry opened at the MK Gallery.

Director Anthony Spira said it was "great" that the city's place on the shortlist had surprised people.

"People who live here absolutely love it. But externally, people are saying, 'Milton Keynes, is there culture there?' Well, yes, there is, there's a lot and there's going to be a lot more."

Spira is confident the city, which was born only 59 years ago, can win: "We've got a very different story."

Entertainment.title: ‘My death was reported in Rolling Stone’: how the Zombies made Time of the Season
Entertainment.text:
Rod Argent, writer, Hammond L100 organ and backing vocals

Our first single, She’s Not There, was one of the first songs I wrote, when I was 18. It remained our only hit in the UK by the time we recorded our second album, Odessey and Oracle, in 1967 – this was only three years later but it felt like a lifetime. We’d recently signed to CBS and had been given £1,000, which even then was not a huge amount of money. We recorded pretty quickly in a few sessions spread over six months, producing ourselves for the first time.

Time of the Season was the last song I wrote for the album. I was sharing a flat with our bass player Chris White, and we were going to each other’s rooms and playing the different things we had. I said: “I think I’ve just written a song that could be a hit.”

The lyrics reflected the mood of the time. In 1967 there were pictures of war on TV, and people were seeing what a devastating thing it was and saying: “I’m not going to be part of this.” The “Who’s your daddy?” line was, in a way, going back to Gershwin’s Summertime, one of the first songs we performed together, but “Is he rich like me?” had kind of a double meaning: “rich” in the sense of understanding how to live.

We recorded at EMI Recording Studios, later known as Abbey Road. The Beatles were in before us making Sgt Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band – we had the benefit of some of the same recording engineers, in particular Geoff Emerick. He found this special way of marrying the bass and the tom-tom sound. I suggested the clap before the beat and a vocal sound after, which became the exhalation.

We soon used up our £1,000, but because of the tight timeframe we were working to, there was a spontaneity and freshness that was very valuable. It’s a method I try to preserve. It’s just much more fun.

Colin Blunstone, lead and backing vocals

I was learning Time of the Season while we recorded it. Standing where the vocal mic had been set up, I was looking at this big red recording light with a clock underneath it while I tried to get it right. The studio was very strict about sessions finishing on time, and there were these guys with long brown coats moving equipment about. On one occasion, we were standing around a piano working out harmonies and they wheeled it out in the middle of a take.

Rod always has an overview of his songs in his head – he can hear the drum track, what the bass should be playing and what the lead vocal should be doing. He’s extremely good at phrasing, so he was in the control room saying: “No, this phrase should be on the beat but the next phrase should be pushed …” Meanwhile, all the time I’m watching the big hand creeping towards five o’clock.

Things got a little bit heated. I was saying, “If you’re so bloody good, you come in here and sing it,” and he said, “You’re the bloody lead singer, you stand in there until you get it right!” The language was probably richer than that. It makes me smile now to think I was breaking off from saying the most terrible things to Rod to sing these angelic lines: “It’s the time of the season for loving …”

Rod likes to think I disliked Time of the Season, but I just thought there were more commercial songs on the album. Care of Cell 44, to me, sounded like the epitome of a hit single, but obviously I was wrong – it was released ahead of Odessey and Oracle and wasn’t successful. By the time the album came out in Terry Quirk’s misspelled sleeve, the band had split.

The following year, Al Kooper left the American band Blood, Sweat & Tears and became a staff producer at CBS. He’d just visited London where he bought about 80 albums that weren’t available in the US, and later said Odessey and Oracle was the one that really stood out. On his first day at CBS he went to see the label’s president, Clive Davis, and said: “Whatever it costs, we have to get this album.” And Davis said: “We already have it. We were going to pass on it – it’s not commercial.”

Al fought for it, and CBS released two singles that disappeared without trace. I think Time of the Season was only put out as a favour to Al, but one DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it, and that was where our luck turned. It gradually picked up huge radio interest.

By then, it was well over a year since we’d broken up and we were all doing other things, but we soon heard that a couple of other bands had started touring the US as the Zombies – one included two members of ZZ Top. The manager of one of these bands claimed they were the original members with a new singer, because Colin Blunstone had been killed in a car crash. It turned out my death was reported in Rolling Stone.

The original Zombies didn’t play together again until 1997, when a box set was launched at the Jazz Cafe in London. I was singing with my solo band, but the other guys came up on stage and let it be known they wanted to play – we hadn’t planned it or rehearsed. We did She’s Not There and Time of the Season and it sounded really good. I thought: “You know what? There really was something special about that band.”

Can you say a song’s got legs? Time of the Season wasn’t a success in the UK charts, but people know it. It’s often used in films set in the 1960s but also appears in commercials, where it sounds really current. I’ve never quite worked out how it can be both of its time and timeless.

Entertainment.title: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America
Entertainment.text:
When I see a film a second time during its theatrical run, it’s typically to take someone else who hasn’t yet seen it, at least in part hoping to witness their reaction to a piece of art that excited or moved me in some way. Seeing Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s You Can See Everything a second time in New York City on a Saturday night was that impulse writ larger. This is a movie garnering a surprisingly sizable audience, and outsized audience reactions to go along with it; rewatching it in a full 300-seat auditorium offered the opportunity to re-experience that sense of discovery. Perhaps more to the point, almost everyone I knew had seen it already; all I could do was observe strangers.

This documentary, peering into (and helping to create) a hall of mirrors around the famed med-tech scammer Elizabeth Holmes, has become the box office story of the fall, actually rising 25% on its second weekend to gross another $19.5m – a rare feat even given its expanded screen count. With over $45m in North America, it’s already one of A24’s biggest movies ever; it could wind up in the company’s top three, and way up on the list of the highest-grossing nonfiction features. If You Can See Everything isn’t quite an Obsession-level cash cow, it’s probably even more surprising that a three-hour documentary whose existence was only announced about eight weeks ago is on track to make more money than high-profile new releases like Practical Magic 2, Verity and Street Fighter, among others. It’s also outgrossed co-director Oppenheim’s fellow A24 surprise hit Primetime, which has the benefit of genuine movie star Robert Pattinson.

A few of the viewers I spoke with following the 8pm showing of You Can See Everything at New York’s AMC Empire (typically one of the highest-grossing venues in the country for any number of new releases, where Everything is currently showing on three to five screens depending on the time of day) had also seen Primetime, aware of the connection between the two films. Just as many, however, were not high-frequency moviegoers, at least not by New York standards. Despite an obviously youthful demographic – perhaps owing to the high tolerance for hustle and/or bustle required to trek out to Times Square, I couldn’t find anyone over 30 – there were several viewers who hadn’t been to the movies in months. (The answer to the question of what movie they last saw in theaters ranged from the month-old Primetime to the obligatory summer mega-blockbuster The Odyssey to, yes, Obsession.) Hardly anyone claimed to be a documentary aficionado, either; no one cited a recent documentary they had seen in theaters, saying they were more likely to catch that sort of thing on streaming, if at all.

So what drew them to a big-screen experience featuring both an entertainer (Nathan Fielder) and a subject (Elizabeth Holmes) more closely associated with television? Most of the twentysomethings I spoke with had some combination of familiarity with Fielder’s more overtly comic work – one woman said this seemed “on brand” for him – and awareness of the notoriety of Holmes, the latter usually stemming from the non-documentary TV series The Dropout, which also figures into the film. Each seemed to provide a surprise hook for a big-screen feature – like a more thoughtful version of seeing a movie because it has Anne Hathaway or Spider-Man (not that there’s anything wrong with following either of those into the dark). To a cinema diehard, this seemed almost counterintuitive; were people really being enticed into theaters by faces they knew largely from couch-bound TV binges? Was this effectively serving as a three-hour crossover between The Dropout and The Rehearsal?

There was a sense that this unexpected team-up was part of the sell, with the WTF nature of that idea intact. The extra promise, though, seemed to be that You Can See Everything would offer something more surprising and less easily spoiled than a typical streaming event. The 23-year-old sitting next to me said that she got the impression from social media – specifically, clips on Instagram and TikTok – that this was “a cultural moment”, as she put it. Multiple viewers echoed that sentiment about seeing a handful of clips via social media, and hearing buzz indicating that the movie simply was “unlike anything else out [at the movies]” and had to be seen firsthand to be believed - or at least to be experienced with the proper amount of spoiler-free, audience-vibing surprise. Remarkably, though the movie had been out for over a week and already discoursed at least halfway to death online, none of these twentysomething viewers reported having any idea about the unexpected pivot the movie made at its halfway mark – especially impressive given that it involves another marquee name added to the mix.

During the movie itself, that mystery guest felt like she was winning fans in real time; she even got a round of spontaneous applause by describing Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, as “batshit crazy”. But while early screenings had been described as meeting with rapturous audience engagement driven by the film’s surprises, this one felt more unpredictable in its alternating waves of laughter and murmuring discomfort. Early in the film, Holmes gets teary talking about the potential separation from her children as she prepares to leave for her prison sentence in a few weeks. Both times I’ve watched it with a full audience, Fielder’s reaction – “that must be hard” – drew one of the movie’s biggest laughs, seemingly for how flatly obligatory it sounds. Yet if this moment primed the audience for peals of cringe-comedy laughter or outright derision toward either Fielder’s affect or Holmes’s refusal to accept responsibility for her deception, that’s not exactly how the movie played out. The movie often cuts to Fielder lurking within proximity of the Holmes family during tense moments; though the mechanics of these de facto reaction shots are similar, sometimes they drew big laughs and sometimes what felt more like hushed suspense. It was as if viewers were deciding moment to moment whether they were watching dark comedy or something more menacing. Though the disparaging of Evans got an enthusiastically cathartic reaction, applause when the movie threw to its end credits was scattered and uncertain.

It’s not unprecedented for a movie to garner audibly mixed reactions. But something Oppenheim and Fielder seem to have cracked is allowing an audience to feel satisfied and impressed by those reactions, which would often serve as a death knell to a prospective blockbuster. When I asked people after the show for their immediate impressions of the film, one woman said it was “funnier than I expected”, while another was surprised by the sympathy she felt for Holmes at times despite feeling “on guard” about what to believe from her.

The most common reaction, however, was a kind of admiring confusion. They weren’t exactly sure what to think, a feeling that’s not traditionally music to a film executive’s ears. Because its initial release was in fewer than a thousand theaters, You Can See Everything hasn’t been subjected to the traditional and finicky CinemaScore polling that asks opening-night audiences for a grade, and seems to inexplicably augur disappointment with anything that’s not at least a B+. But PostTrak, another polling service, shows highly positive results. This could carry the movie past the $100m mark in North America, something only ever accomplished by one other documentary: Michael Moore’s hot-button Fahrenheit 9/11, which had the advantage of election-year currency and a film-maker coming off an Oscar win.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.

The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.

Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.

The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.

"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.

Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.

In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.

Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.

It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder.

Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.

It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.

The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.

The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.

The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."

"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.

"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.

"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.

The review is due to report in five months.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Israelis and Americans are both voting - with global consequences
BreakingNewsTab.text:
In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.

By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.

Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.

A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.

For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.

The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.

And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.

Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and much of the world's energy supply.

The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.

He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.

His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.

US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.

"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Drivers jailed over deaths of mum and daughter in Leeds
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed.

Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her daughter Lena Czepczor were killed when they were hit by an Audi TT RS as they walked to the girl's nursery on the A61 Scott Hall Road on 16 January 2023.

At Leeds Crown Court on Monday, Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was jailed for 12 years and Jasskamal Riyat, 37, for 16 years.

Sentencing the men, Judge Singh said the road was "not a race track" and told them the deaths had consequences that were "immeasurable", with an "immense" impact on those left behind.

Bhachu, of Grant Row in Adel, had earlier admitted two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, while Riyat, of Buckstone Avenue in Moortown, was convicted by a jury after denying he had been racing him.

The court heard the pair, who did not previously know each other, accelerated away from traffic lights on Scott Hall Road shortly before the crash.

Prosecutors said Riyat's BMW reached speeds of up to 89mph in the 40mph zone before Bhachu lost control of his Audi, mounted the pavement and struck Hulboj and her daughter.

Judge Singh said the victims had "done nothing wrong" and were "simply walking to school".

Addressing the defendants, he said: "A road is not a race track. A powerful car is not an invitation to test its limits on a public road.

"The consequences of competitive driving at extreme speed can be, and in this case were, irreversible."

He added: "Justyna and Lena should have gone to school that morning. They should have returned home. They should have continued with their lives.

"Instead, their lives ended on a pavement because two drivers chose to drive in a manner which placed speed and competition above the safety of everyone around them."

Susannah Proctor, for Bhachu, told the court that her client was a "normal person who's made a massive mistake".

She said he "must live with himself in the knowledge of the devastation he has caused".

And she said: "He did not intend to cause this devastation but cause it he has."

Hulboj's fiancé Dominik Czepczor watched the sentencing hearing in court.

A statement from him was read, which said: "My whole world collapsed in one second.

"Every day I feel a huge void after their departure.

"We had so many hopes and dreams and in one moment it all ended.

"My dream was to have a wonderful family, and I must say that it came true for a short while, but that was taken away from me on January 16.

"Unfortunately, all that remains are wonderful memories and a constant fight for the next day, which is not easy."

Det Insp Paul Conroy, of West Yorkshire Police's Major Collision Enquiry Team, said: "A woman and her young daughter have died because of the actions of these men, and I know no sentence will ever feel enough to compensate for the lives that have been lost.

"This sentencing hearing though does mark the end of a long criminal justice process for Justyna and Lena's family.

"It is over two years since Bhachu admitted his part in this tragic incident and I know that the wait for justice has taken its toll.

"My thoughts are firmly with them today."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Storm Boelo clean-up begins as thousands left without power
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 22,600 properties are still without power as of Monday afternoon.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.

The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for strong winds from 18:00 on Monday to 03:00 on Tuesday across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland.

The Met Office has warned that further power cuts in areas covered by the warning are likely and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

Coastal communities could also be affected by spray or large waves, while travel delays are expected.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," Slade told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

Marcus Reed, the operations director at a home fragrance manufacturer, said his factory and shop in Lyndal, Cumbria would be without power until Tuesday evening.

He told the Today programme that he has had to turn away employees and customers.

"To lose two days manufacturing and distribution is going to be really disruptive," he said, adding that it was bad timing as it was "the busiest time of the year" for his business in the lead-up to Christmas.

"This is probably the worst situation I've experienced in my time here; we've had ad hoc issues over weekends where we've lost power, but it's been contained within a 12-hour period. It's the first time anything like this has happened, it's very serious."

Wendy McKinney, whose bathroom shop in the seaside town of Largs in North Ayrshire was flooded on Sunday, told the Today programme the storm had been "devastating to local businesses".

She said the local council only handed out sandbags after flooding had already started:"[They] were just left in the middle of the street yesterday afternoon on pallets just for everybody just to try and help themselves, but it was too little too late."

North Ayrshire Council told the BBC that it had distributed almost 300 sandbags in Largs and Saltcoats and would continue to "respond where it has been safe and appropriate to do so".

A spokesperson said council teams "followed established resilience procedures" but would review flooding reports and "consider any lessons that can be learned".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Chris Brown: US singer given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
BreakingNewsTab.text:
US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.

The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.

Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.

Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".

The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.

The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.

In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."

CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.

Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."

The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."

He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.

The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone".

But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".

Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July.

The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.

These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.

Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head.

"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."

Judge Baumgartner told the pair that while he had concluded they had both crossed the threshold to be jailed, this year's changes to sentencing laws meant that he had to put off doing so, unless there were exceptional reasons.

"I have considered whether the seriousness of the offending, taken together with the need for punishment and deterrence, amounts to exceptional circumstances requiring immediate imprisonment. I have concluded, in relation to each of you, that it does not," he said.

"These were serious offences deserving of custodial sentences, but the circumstances do not justify displacing the [new legal] requirement that those sentences be suspended."

On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.

The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.

Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.

The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.

The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".

The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.

The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".

Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack.

"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said.

"It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20.

"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."

The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.

Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.

She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."

Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".

An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.

Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.

The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.

Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.

Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.

There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.

After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.

Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.

Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up.

BreakingNewsTab.title: John Healey's Budget to shield low-income pensioners from income tax
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Pensioners on low incomes will be shielded from income tax by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget on Wednesday.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to increase by 3.9% to £13,036.40 a year from April. This would take the payment above the £12,570 personal tax allowance and therefore be liable for income tax if no changes are made.

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension. Healey will explain this pledge will be met by plans for a new tax allowance for low-income pensioners.

Healey's plans come as the Conservatives and Reform UK unveil their alternative Budget proposals, including deep cuts to the welfare bill.

The chancellor's allies argue his plans for pensioners will mean they do not need to face an administrative burden just to pay a small amount of tax.

More specific details, including how many pensioners this will affect, have yet to be confirmed by the Treasury.

The Budget is due to be printed this evening, with Healey's speech likely to be fine-tuned right up until it is delivered on Wednesday lunchtime.

Treasury sources concede it will not involve the scale of tax and spending announcements seen from Labour and Conservative governments in recent years.

The Tories are calling on the chancellor to cut green taxes, red tape and benefits to bring down energy bills.

Reform is recommending the chancellor adopts 60 policies which they claim will create jobs - including approving the controversial Rosebank oil field - a project Healey is understood to back.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper has called on the government to agree a new growth and defence partnership with the EU, including joining the single market. She argued this would help "ease the huge tax burden weighing people down".

The Green Party has urged Healey to use his first Budget to "make the UK affordable", including by funding energy bill support by ending a tax relief for data centres.

Senior Green politicians, including leader Zack Polanski, MPs and peers, made clear their suggestions in a letter to Healey.

BreakingNewsTab.title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.

Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".

But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.

He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."

"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.

"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."

She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.

The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.

In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.

However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries.

The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.

Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had.

"For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.

The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.

However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".

Farage told broadcasters he was "up for the fight again" on the EU and an "election is coming" to decide that.

"Crucially, [Burnham] goes to Brussels on 20 November for a key summit - he must not sign up to anything there without at least putting those minor changes to a general election," he said.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Russell Brand asked assistant for female fan phone numbers, court hears
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A former personal assistant of Russell Brand has told a court she was instructed to get phone numbers for the entertainer from female fans when she first started working with him.

Helen Berger, who worked closely with Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, said the request "felt uncomfortable" and, after seeking advice, she told the TV personality that she would not do that anymore.

Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

Brand had an "insane sexual appetite", Berger told Southwark Crown Court in a written statement on Monday.

Berger left her job with Brand after she became "sick of him", she said. She added that he had sex with numerous women during the time she was his assistant.

She described a work environment where Brand would ask her if he could "go and have sex now" when frustrated with a particular task.

Berger added that she never "witnessed anything against the law" but that "everyone normalised and dismissed his behaviour" so it "made me think it was accepted."

She told the court that "peacock" Brand found random women online to satisfy his "insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night", but sex often made him depressed.

She told the court Brand used MySpace to find women for sex, and said: "At his house, women often came over and it was clear they were there for sex."

She recalled once finding a female celebrity asleep in Brand's bed while he was wandering around the house half-dressed, and said of the comedian: "He was like a peacock, women would always approach him."

Russell Brand's defence team says any sexual activity was consensual and accounts have been twisted in the light of a defamatory TV documentary in 2023 which made allegations of sexual abuse against the entertainer.

The prosecution is due to finish on Tuesday morning.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Bristol woman wins £127k High Court claim for mum's care at home
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A woman has described her "phenomenal" relief after she won a legal case that means she is entitled to be paid £127k from her mother's estate for caring for her in her final years.

Bern Rogers, from Bristol, told the BBC of the "harrowing and deeply sad" family dispute since her elderly mother Sheila died in 2020, which led to her facing criminal charges.

Legal experts said the "hugely significant" High Court ruling would lead to other claims.

The executor of Sheila's estate, Bern's brother Andrew, said it had "always been willing to pay" her "genuine expenses" and an extra amount for her efforts. But the estate intends to appeal against the judgment that awarded Bern £127,500 for care provided.

Bern looked after Sheila, who had dementia, for two-and-a-half years.

After Sheila moved into Bern's house in Bristol in September 2017, she wanted to be cared for by her daughter rather than get costly home care or go into a residential care home.

Crucially, Bern said she agreed with her mother she would be paid for the round-the-clock care.

After Sheila died in April 2020, Bern took £100,000 from her estate. It led to her being reported to the police for fraud and theft.

The money was seized and Bern was charged. But, at a trial at Bristol Crown Court in 2022, she was found not guilty by a jury.

After being cleared, Bern turned to the civil courts.

In 2025, a High Court judge ruled she had entered into an informal contract with Sheila for payment of a reasonable sum for her care.

The estate was also ordered by a judge to pay Bern's legal costs.

In August this year, another High Court judge worked out the amount Bern was due and ruled she was owed £127,500 for the 850 days of care she provided.

"Mum came to live with me, she became very confused and was seen wandering in the garden and obviously needed care," Bern said. "We didn't know what was wrong with her."

She said caring for her mother had been like a full-time job, adding: "I couldn't leave her really. She became unpredictable."

Sheila became more frail, was diagnosed with dementia and also had a series of physical health problems, including a "chronic" and "disabling" prolapse.

Bern's husband Jon said: "It was relentless after she moved in with us. We couldn't go out even to the shops. It was a 24-hour job.

"It was a privilege, but we had to put our lives on hold for more than two years and revolve our lives around looking after her."

He remembered that in Sheila's final weeks, his wife was sleeping on the floor of her mother's bedroom to make sure she was alright.

Bern said "of course" she would have looked after her mother if she had not been able to pay her.

But she said her mother had wanted to be looked after by her daughter rather than getting professional carers or going into a home, which would have cost thousands of pounds a month.

"She was very insistent and would tell anyone that would listen that she wanted to make sure that I sorted out money for her care, I was to make sure I got paid properly," she said.

Multiple messages from Bern's five siblings were shown in court saying that she should be paid something for the care, although no amount was agreed.

That is why, she explained, shortly after her mother had died, she transferred £100,000 from her mother's account.

Bern was reported to the police for theft and fraud, which she describes as a "terrible and devastating betrayal".

"It has been harrowing and deeply sad for it to go from a normal family relationship to being treated like a scapegoat, five against one," she said.

After the two separate High Court judgements in her favour, Bern said: "The weight off my shoulders was phenomenal.

"It has been absolutely wonderful to be vindicated. It means I can get on with my life now, the rest of my retirement."

Jon said: "I'm very proud of her, actually, because she has stuck up for her mother, for carers and for herself.

"It's been a very long and tough journey of nine years, and we've finally got justice."

Bern said she was "terribly proud" that her case could influence others in future, which she said was her mum's "legacy".

"It's a huge win for carers everywhere," Jon added, but stressed families still needed to have open discussions about what was fair.

The ruling that states that Bern is entitled to payment cannot be appealed against, however, the estate intends to lodge an appeal against the second ruling that decided the amount owed.

The executor of Sheila's estate is Bern's brother, Andrew Wills. In a statement on behalf of the estate, he said: "The only agreements that we (her siblings) were aware of was for my mother to give Bernadette £50 per week 'keep' and to ensure that Bernadette was not to be out of pocket.

"We were not made aware of any other contract between our mother and Bernadette."

The statement added: "At all times I have attempted to be independent and to act in the best interests of the estate.

"The estate has always been willing to pay Bernadette her genuine expenses as well as an additional gratuity in recognition of her efforts for our mother.

"We have always tried to be fair. Unfortunately, our offers were not accepted by Bernadette who instead issued legal proceedings against the estate."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Brazil election: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic comeback over Bolsonaro
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.

Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting.

Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy".

Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election.

Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same.

But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed.

Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias.

But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason.

Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to miss out.

The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques – appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race.

The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies - 4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult to challenge.

The result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%.

The right-wing candidate had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable".

But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one.

Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989.

As disconsolate Bolsonaro supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate and address his supporters.

"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker said. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people."

Vice-President Geraldo Alckmin told him: "You, for the second time, have saved Brazilian democracy."

Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans.

Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023.

His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030.

But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from the US president.

Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard".

Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support.

Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Serbia's veteran ruler Vučić concedes election to student-led protest movement
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.

Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities.

The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society.

"It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader Vučić said as he conceded. With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.25 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.

The students had secured 52.7% of the vote, while Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.

Vučić had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.

During a celebration speech, Student List candidate Radomir Saicic said Serbians had shown "no obstacle was greater than their will", Reuters reported. "No force can forever overpower a people who have decided to take their destiny into their own hands," he added.

Amid scenes of people dancing in the streets Belgrade, Selena Lebovic said the result was "really fabulous".

"We are all crying, and what to say. We couldn't believe that it would be so easy," she told Reuters.

Vučić made his announcement at the headquarters of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the capital Belgrade.

The centre of Novi Sad - the northern city that triggered the student-led protests - was crowded. "Everything is going to get better now," David Vasić, one of those celebrating, told BBC Serbian.

The Student List - which has no obvious leaders and whose members are not used to politics - had attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

It decided to field candidates to the 250-member parliament from across Serbian society including doctors, actors, academics and sports personalities.

"This is not an ordinary election victory, this is an avalanche that has wiped out an authoritarian regime and entire political scene," said Nebojša Vladisavljević, professor of political science at the University of Belgrade.

There were now two big political groups in Serbia, and the Student List had "absolute legitimacy" to govern for the coming years, he told BBC Serbian.

European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said "a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together".

Earlier in the day, long queues were seen outside polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia.

This was also the case outside booths in a number of countries with sizeable Serbian communities - including Slovenia's capital Ljubljana, Germany's Munich, and Los Angeles and Chicago in the US.

In France, Serbian voters waited in line in heavy rain in Paris.

The election was held amid high tensions across Serbia, with police sealing off streets around the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) in Belgrade.

Attention will now turn to who will lead the Student List as prime minister. Presidential elections are due to take place in December, with parliament speaker Ana Brnabić currently filling the role in a caretaker capacity.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.

Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.

Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".

Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the administration's immigration policies. But Trump has typically enjoyed the support of Catholic voters.

In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons".

"In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said.

"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.

A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media.

Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump.

Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants.

"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote.

"I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added.

Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event.

When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops.

"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.

According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.

That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.

During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.

Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".

They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."

The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.

Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.

A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.
