articles.title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
articles.text:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.

That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.

Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around £24bn to as low as £11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.

The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.

At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.

Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.

BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown has called on Healey to hike the tax on electronic gaming machines - such as those found in betting shops and adult gaming centres which can offer payouts of £500 per game - citing the social harm imposed by problem gambling.

The Social Market Foundation (SMF) think tank has estimated, external that doubling tax on these machines from 20% to 40% could raise could raise between £275m and £460m - depending on how gamblers reacted to it.

People who use gambling machines could also end up having the tax passed on to them through worse odds on games, though anti-gambling groups argue this could help discourage more people from using them.

Research from the SMF found that gambling machines are increasingly clustered on some of the UK's most deprived high streets, and that one in four people who play casino games on these machines gamble at risky or harmful levels.

Reports suggest the chancellor is preparing to announce that big online marketplaces such as Amazon, Ebay and Temu will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by retailers selling on their platforms.

The Treasury estimates it is missing out on around £12bn a year, external in VAT revenues that should be paid by companies, which it calls the "VAT tax gap".

Tax experts say that part of the problem - although not accounting for the full £12bn of the VAT gap - is that some online sellers fail to comply with VAT rules, either by not charging VAT when they should or by failing to pass on VAT collected from customers to the government.

Enforcement can be difficult because some firms that use platforms like Amazon to sell their products are based overseas and falsely present themselves as UK-established businesses.

Others close down and reopen under different company names to escape their tax liabilities.

Reports suggest that this move to make big online marketplaces responsible for collecting the tax - rather than the individual retailers - would clamp down on this form of tax evasion and could raise around £1bn in extra VAT a year.

Amazon, which supports the move, has estimated it could raise £700m, external a year in VAT for the government.

Some sellers could respond by raising prices or leaving the platform, which could have an impact on some shoppers.

However, it would also level the playing field for online sellers, ensuring those businesses who charge VAT are not illegally undercut by those who break the rules and do not.

Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves attempted to reduce spending on these benefits , externalby £5bn a year by 2030, but were forced to reverse course after a revolt by backbench Labour MPs.

Independent welfare experts and economists say savings from the working age welfare budget are possible but would likely require upfront spending to help people into work, which could cancel out any near-term savings for the Treasury.

Cuts to health and disability welfare would reduce the incomes of people who currently receive those payments, external and/or those who would otherwise receive them in future - and campaigners warn of the risk of people being pushed into poverty.

However, if more welfare claimants were also supported into work, their overall incomes could be maintained or even rise.

Graphics by Callum Thomson and Lewis McBlane.

articles.title: Anthropic reveals rapid revenue gains and larger losses in stock market filing
articles.text:
Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.

Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, confidentially filed with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.

“We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’s investor prospectus reads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction.

A leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is its flagship product, which offers text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEO Dario Amodei founded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.

Anthropic’s audited filings will offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of a potential AI bubble swirl.

The company detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.

Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.

Anthropic has focused on businesses as its primary paying customers, unlike OpenAI, which has courted everyday consumers for ChatGPT. As of 30 September, Anthropic said it had more than 14,000 enterprise customers – 11,900 of which had $100,000 or more of revenue, more than 1,900 that had $1m or more revenue and about 250 enterprise customers that had $10m or more revenue.

“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” Anthropic executives wrote.

The filing contains some of the hyperbolic language characteristic of AI companies predicting the miraculous potential of their technology. Describing the potential of AI agents, semi-autonomous chatbots that can carry out tasks on behalf of users, Anthropic executives wrote: “The result is something without historical precedent: what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a datacenter, available to every organization and sector of the economy.”

Investing in Anthropic and the development of a model that the company claims could revolutionize knowledge work across industries comes with a great deal of risk. Anthropic listed more than 90 pages of potential to its business. For one, a “substantial portion” of the company’s revenue comes from a limited number of customers, and losing any of them could put a huge dent in their revenue. A quarter of Anthropic’s revenue comes from its top five customers, though no single customer represents more than 10% of its business.

The company also has incurred $6.2bn in debt as it built out its infrastructure and spends billions yearly on computing power provided by third parties, according to the filing.

The misuse of AI and Claude in particular also poses a considerable risk to Anthropic’s business. When it comes to AI, there are four categories of potential risk, executives wrote: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. Anthropic’s most capable models have “capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote. The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended.”

Amodei has called for a slowdown of AI’s development, citing existential risk. Anthropic’s stock market listing may elicit a rush of investment in the company and the AI sector more broadly, which could speed up the pace of the industry further.

The company disclosed that in September 2025, staffers documented what they believe was the first large-scale cyber-attack that didn’t rely on significant human intervention. Anthropic “detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”.

Donald Trump’s administration may also be a risk to the company. Anthropic has been embroiled in a feud with the Trump administration over the use of the startup’s products in warfare, which culminated in the designation of the company as a supply chain risk, a first for an American company. This prevents any military agency from contracting with Anthropic. The company has challenged the blacklisting.

articles.title: Anthropic files for stock market IPO; Meta announces $95bn fundraising drive to pay for AI expansion – as it happened
articles.text:
Meta to raise $95bn to help fund AI plans

Boom! Meta has just announced plans to raise up to $95bn to help pay for its massive AI ambitions.

The company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is kicking off a new fundraising drive to fund “its core business and emerging AI opportunities”.

The fundraising comes in two parts.

First, Meta plans to raise $35bn through new “underwritten public offerings” – a sale of company stock.

This offering has some big name backers – Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have all shown interest in taking part, Meta says. These ‘cornerstone investors’ could buy up to $5bn of the stock on offer.

Second, Meta also plans to launch a $60bn “at-the-market offering” – in which it will sell new common stock to investors at the going market rate in future.

The Silicon Valley giant says these plans will support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”.

It also says it is “investing with financial discipline,” saying:

double quotation markAI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services. Meta’s AI investments are already generating tangible returns through increased engagement, improved advertising performance and increased monetization. Meta is also pursuing new opportunities across personal superintelligence, consumer and business agents, enterprise products, and AI glasses.

The ‘at the market offering’ involves selling Meta’s new Class C Stock, which it announced last week it is creating. These Class C shares don’t have voting rights, so can be sold without diluting founder Mark Zuckerberg’s control of the company.

Internal forecasts last week showed that Meta needs to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” over several years to fund its AI plans.

Anthropic has fired the starting gun on the AI pioneer’s bid to join the stock market, with a warning about the risks that its technology poses.

Anthropic made its long-awaited filing for a public offering today – it hopes to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.

The IPO document showed that Anthropic made a loss of $80bn in the first half the year (mainly due to changes in the value of bonds which can convert into its stock), on revenues of over $16bn.

The company also warned of the risks from AI, including the danger that AI is used for cybercrime or to design biological weapons, misused by authoritarian states, or that humans could lose control of it.

The IPO filing came on a busy day for the tech sector, with Meta announcing plans to raise up to $95bn through new stock sales.

The money would be used to fund its AI ambitions:

Elon Musk grabbed the early spotlight, warning that some AI cloud computing companies were being locked out of the debt markets.

double quotation mark“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers.”

There was also drama on the Brazilian stock market, where shares plunged after president Lula won a fourth term in power.

Elsewhere in the markets, European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.

Anthropic is attempting to float on the stock market just five years after it was created.

In today’s IPO filing, the company warns that its “limited operating history” makes it hard to evaluate its future prospects (especially as AI is “an evolving and nascent industry”). “This increases the risk that we will not be successful,” it says.

Anthropic then lists a series of “risks and challenges”

develop and release new models and products on a timely and cost-effective basis;

accurately forecast our revenue, operating expenses, and compute requirements in an environment characterized by rapid technological change and usage patterns that may scale in nonlinear or exponential ways;

secure access to sufficient compute to meet the needs of all our workloads and manage the risks related to securing compute;

effectively manage our growth, including our cash flows and capital needs;

accurately predict customer demands, expectations, or requirements;

maintain and enhance our brand and reputation;

attract, retain, utilize, and motivate our highly skilled personnel;

build and maintain our strategic partnerships;

anticipate and respond to macroeconomic changes and changes in the industry and markets in which we operate;

anticipate and respond to evolving regulatory requirements and political dynamics;

maintain our safety-focused approach while meeting market demands;

successfully monetize our models, platform, and applications; and

respond effectively to competitive threats.

Anthropic: We may face litigation over AI harms

Looking back at the Anthropic IPO document…. and the AI firm has included a clear warning about the dangers of its technology.

“Our AI models may themselves cause harm by producing undesirable outputs or behaving in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking unintended or harmful actions that no user or third party directed,” Anthropic explains.

These risks may increase as Anthropic’s models become more capable, it says, and as they are deployed in high-risk or sensitive contexts – from scientific research to government.

This could lead to legal action, Anthropic states:

double quotation markWe may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models, and our contractual protections and insurance may be insufficient, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Report: Cost of living pressures driven up by high oil price

Pressure on John Healey to provide more support at the budget to the most vulnerable in society is only going to become more intense with the price of a barrel of Brent crude still above $110.

A new report from a longstanding study of the impact of cost of living pressures on low income families, shows that parents struggle to pay the costs of transporting disabled children to school and health appointments.

Those in employment are also affected getting to and from work in a car when petrol is above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre. It can mean that work doesn’t pay, says the report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.

Patrick runs the changing realities project that follows 100 low income families.

Rosie L, who lives in a couple household in rural Scotland, said:

double quotation mark“... it’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car, we live rurally. Absolutely have to have a car and public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are ... Not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly, as my children are disabled.”

The latest report involves in-depth interviews with 70 participants of which 67 shared strategies taken to reduce costs over the previous month.

double quotation mark“Nearly three-quarters (73%) had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold. More than two-thirds (68%) had gone without buying something they needed for their children, such as new shoes or a winter coat. Just over half (51%) had visited a food bank or used other forms of charitable food provision, while 40% had borrowed money from family and friends. Almost half of parents (49%) had also said no to their children’s requests for educational or after-school activities.”

Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities, so far, did not match the scale of the problem.

double quotation mark“The Budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’. Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of Child Benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

Brazilian stock market plunges 17% after Lula's win

Stocks are plunging on the Brazilian stock market, as investors react to leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s victory over his far-right opponent Flávio Bolsonaro in last weekend’s presidential election.

The Ibovespa share index, of leading companies listed in Brazil, has tumbled by 17% in a chaotic start that saw trading briefly halted.

Lale Akoner, global market strategist for etoro, explains:

double quotation mark“Lula’s re-election could keep Brazilian stocks and the currency under pressure in the near term, but the sharp sell-off may also create opportunities for investors. Markets had largely expected a Bolsonaro victory, so part of the reaction reflects investors rapidly reversing their positions rather than a sudden deterioration in Brazil’s economy.”

Investors had expected a Bolsonaro victory, and some are concerned that Lula is less likely to try to rein in Brazil’s borrowing.

Viktor Szabó, investment director for emerging market debt at Aberdeen Investments, says:

double quotation markLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva has completed one of the most remarkable comebacks in Brazil’s democratic history. Three weeks after finishing second in the first round, he won Sunday’s run-off with 51.8% of valid votes against 48.2% for Flávio Bolsonaro. He is the first candidate since the return of democracy to win the presidency after trailing in the first round, and the first Brazilian to be elected president four times. His new term begins in January.

Markets will take a very different view. Brazilian markets had not opened when this article was written, but a strong negative reaction is expected. Investors had leaned heavily towards a change of government: the Ibovespa rose more than 8% in early trading after the first round and long-term interest rates fell sharply on hopes of a shift in fiscal policy. Much of that move now looks set to reverse, and the burden of proof sits squarely with the re-elected president.

Here’s our liveblog with the latest news from Brazil:

Updated at 10.12 EDT

Although Anthropic wants to sell some of its shares to the public, its founders aren’t planning on losing control.

The company has devised a “Founder Voting Structure” which will give its seven co-founders majority voting control over the company, under a plan outlined last month.

Anthropic explains:

double quotation markWe believe that our seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah, as a group, are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.

Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members (the “Founder LLC”).

Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors.

Anthropic's loss hit $80bn in first half of 2026

Anthropic’s IPO filing thrown a light on the company’s financial performance – where revenues and losses have both been growing at a remarkable rate.

The document filed with the SEC today shows that Antropic pulled in revenues of $16.2bn in the first half of this year, up from just $1.16bn a year earlier.

But losses surged to over $80bn in January-June this year, up from $12.9bn a year before.

That jump in losses was mainly due to a rise in the fair value of convertible notes, which can be converted into stock.

double quotation markWe have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.

Updated at 10.51 EDT

Anthropic files for stock market float

Newsflash: AI firm Anthropic has taken an important step towards floating on the New York Stock Exchange.

In the last few minutes, Anthropic filed publicly for an initial public offering, in which it declares that “AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history”.

If managed well, Anthropic says, it could rapidly speed up scientific discovery, “greatly increase economic growth rates”, help cure major disease and solve other serious problems.

But alongside the potential of AI, Anthropic – which operates the Claude chatbot – also points to the risks – warning that AI can be used “for ill as well as good”.

The word risks appears more than 200 times in the IPO filing – and those risks include the danger that AI is used for cybercrime or to design biological weapons, misused by authoritarian states, or that humans could lose control of it, Anthropic says.

It’s not immediately cleat what value Anthropic is aiming for – the section showing how many shares it will sell, and at what price, is blank….

Updated at 09.20 EDT

Chinese online shopping giant Temu has agreed to take action to reduce the prospect of illegal goods being sold on its platform to comply with EU legislation.

It has now been given four months by the EU to prove it can remedy the breaches of the Digital Services Act.

Following a €200m fine in May, the website will launch a six month risk assessment of products along with an evaluation of the effectiveness of measures put in place to stop illegal products being sold on its platform.

The Chinese platform was warned it would face a series of rolling fines if it it did not do this.

Among the items the EU found on its website were baby dummies posing a choke hazard, clothing and jewellery with carcinogenic chemicals and electrical chargers failing basic safety tests.

SpaceX enters $4bn deal with Apollo for AI chips

Newsflash: We have another multi-billion dollar deal in the AI world.

SpaceX has reported that it has agreed to lease data centre hardware, including AI chips, from an entity managed by asset management firm Apollo Global Management.

The equipment will be leased for around five years, and used in data centres selected by SpaceX – which expects to pay roughly $40bn to Apollo under the deal.

The lease schedules are expected to commence during the first half of 2027 upon delivery of the GPUs, SpaceX says in an SEC filing.

Reminder: Elon Musk posted last night that SpaceX had “closed $40B of debt for GPUs”…

Oxford Street finally pedestrianised

On a wetter Monday morning than London’s mayor may have dreamed of, pedestrians walked freely through the temporary bollards onto a green welcome banner rolled along the tarmac, declaring Oxford Street traffic-free.

Sadiq Khan said it was a “momentous day”, with almost a kilometre of the capital’s most famous shopping street now pedestrianised, banishing the buses, bikes, taxis, e-scooters and pedicabs along with the private car.

After decades of discussion, the closure to traffic has come into effect in time for the busy Christmas shopping period, although the bigger transformation of the street, a £150m project including trees, seating and level “plazas” for events, will start taking shape from spring 2027.

Speaking on Monday morning in the John Lewis department store, Khan said he was proud to be “finally unlocking a new era”, noting that the first action plans to pedestrianise the street started in 1971 “when I was literally in nappies”.

The mayor, whose first jobs were in retail in stores in the street, said:

double quotation mark“This is a momentous day for Oxford Street and the capital. We want high quality shops that will atrract people here but also culture, hospitality, leisure, and people going to and from the office having a good experience and I’m confident we’ll get that.”

double quotation mark“We’ve seen over the last couple of decades this street in decline… Pedestrianising the street with great public transport links, more greenery, more seating, will link to a better experience all round.”

The permanent plans will depend on feedback in the first phase and testing, and Khan said London “would be closely monitoring these changes to make sure they are working for everyone”.

He added: “I want this to be a proof of concept – that investing in people rather than traffic leads to better footfall and spend.”

About half of the 1.2 mile street is now vehicle-free, roughly from Oxford Circus station to close to Marble Arch.

Many of London’s double-decker buses have traditionally run the length of the street and will now be diverted into neighbouring roads.

Claire Mann, chief operating officer at Transport for London, said there would still be “plenty of capacity for passengers” and it should not affect reliability. She said:

double quotation mark“People have said for some time it’s an unpleasanat environment to walk along, narrow and busy – the main movement through Oxford Street is pedestrians so this is us enabling people to make that journey in a nicer way. We’ll be monitoring to see if it does have an impact on ridership – but Bond Street and the Elizabeth Line does give you a way to arrive in style.”

Wall Street likes the sound of Meta’s fundraising plan – the company’s shares are up 2% in pre-market trading.

Meta to raise $95bn to help fund AI plans

Boom! Meta has just announced plans to raise up to $95bn to help pay for its massive AI ambitions.

The company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is kicking off a new fundraising drive to fund “its core business and emerging AI opportunities”.

The fundraising comes in two parts.

First, Meta plans to raise $35bn through new “underwritten public offerings” – a sale of company stock.

This offering has some big name backers – Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have all shown interest in taking part, Meta says. These ‘cornerstone investors’ could buy up to $5bn of the stock on offer.

Second, Meta also plans to launch a $60bn “at-the-market offering” – in which it will sell new common stock to investors at the going market rate in future.

The Silicon Valley giant says these plans will support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”.

It also says it is “investing with financial discipline,” saying:

double quotation markAI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services. Meta’s AI investments are already generating tangible returns through increased engagement, improved advertising performance and increased monetization. Meta is also pursuing new opportunities across personal superintelligence, consumer and business agents, enterprise products, and AI glasses.

The ‘at the market offering’ involves selling Meta’s new Class C Stock, which it announced last week it is creating. These Class C shares don’t have voting rights, so can be sold without diluting founder Mark Zuckerberg’s control of the company.

Internal forecasts last week showed that Meta needs to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” over several years to fund its AI plans.

The downturn in UK retail sales has eased this month, new data shows.

The CBI reports that UK retail sales volumes contracted in the year to October at the slowest rate since April 2025.

A net balance of -10% retailers reported that sales dropped over the last year, better than the -55% recorded in September.

Martin Sartorius, lead economist at the CBI, says:

double quotation mark“The ongoing retail sales downturn eased in October, with volumes falling at their slowest annual pace in over a year. Wholesalers and motor traders also saw some signs of activity steadying over the same period. That said, the outlook remains fragile as businesses face headwinds from cautious household spending and higher fuel costs.

articles.title: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears
articles.text:
European gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.

Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating.

The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports the US and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections.

Those reports helped send the oil price as high as $117 a barrel on Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.

Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.

Britain’s energy regulators have said the country is expected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe this winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europe after decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.

The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.

It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid.

Meanwhile, British households face growing energy bills, which are predicted to rise 16% in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual dual fuel bill.

European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.

articles.title: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home
articles.text:
Audi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.

The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.

The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, but it is polling poorly as it struggles with higher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.

Trump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.

Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, has suffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on imports from the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.

It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.

Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.

The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.

Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”

Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.

articles.title: Ballon d'Or blunder causes confusion - Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe articles published
articles.text:
For a moment, it seemed as though Harry Kane's dreams of winning the Ballon d'Or had come true.

It was shortly after 17:15 GMT on Monday when an article from the award's official website titled "Harry Kane wins the 2026 Ballon d'Or" began to circulate online.

It was more than four and a half hours before the winner of the game's most prestigious individual award was due to be announced at a star-studded event at London's Palladium Theatre.

The widespread sharing of the article caused confusion online, with some wondering whether France Football - the organisers of the award - had fallen short at the final hurdle of keeping the winner, who was voted for by journalists at the end of September, under wraps.

That was until further digging on the Ballon d'Or website revealed that some of the other favourites to win the award - Barcelona's Lamine Yamal, Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe, and Lionel Messi of Inter Miami - had also had similar pieces penned and published about them.

Just before 17:40 BST, the articles about Kane and Mbappe had been removed from the website.

It is unclear whether the articles were published by mistake and whether their removal from the website was intentional or part of a damage-control exercise.

Similar articles were also written about London City Lionesses star Alexia Putellas and Barcelona's Ewa Pajor, who are two of the favourites for the corresponding women's award, also taking place on Monday night.

If Kane is to realise his dream and become the first Englishman to win the award since 2001, he will have to wait a little longer to find out.

articles.title: Man Utd: Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on list if Michael Carrick sacked
articles.text:
Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann are emerging as early contenders to become the next Manchester United head coach if Michael Carrick loses his job.

Carrick's position at Old Trafford is under major threat following the club's poor start to the season, with work towards identifying his successor believed to be ongoing.

It is understood Howe and Nagelsmann both feature prominently on the list of candidates the club has explored to potentially replace him, and that both managers are aware of United's interest.

Sources have also indicated Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired at United, but the fact he is under contract would complicate any move for the Spaniard.

Howe, Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte – who is interested in the job – are out of work, making their potential appointments easier.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Newcastle boss Howe is fully open to joining United if Carrick loses his job.

Nagelsmann is available after leaving his job as Germany head coach after the World Cup, while Conte – who has also been linked with Juventus – is open to returning to football after leaving Napoli in May.

Should Carrick be dismissed, the 20-time English top-flight champions will be looking to appoint their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sir Alex Ferguson departed the club in 2013 on the back of winning their most recent title.

Here, BBC Sport takes a closer look at the contenders who could be up for the job.

articles.title: LIV Golf: Former US Open champion Graeme McDowell confirms exit
articles.text:
Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell has become the latest major champion to confirm his departure from LIV Golf.

The 2010 US Open winner, McDowell, 47, announced on Monday he has "decided not to pursue" LIV 2.0, the new version of the breakaway tour which is due to start in 2027.

Major winners Jon Rahm and Louis Oosthuizen have also confirmed their departures, while McDowell's fellow countryman Tom McKibbin said he was exiting LIV to return to the DP World Tour last week.

England's Tyrrell Hatton and Ian Poulter have also left the competition.

Saudi's Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing from LIV in April - having pumped in more than $5bn (£3.8bn) - leading to the league filing for bankruptcy protection in the United States last month.

It has secured a possible $300m (£224m) in financing from BC Partners Credit to try to move forward with 'LIV 2.0', but only a handful of players have so far committed.

Former world number four McDowell joined LIV when it launched as a lucrative Saudi Arabia-backed project in 2022.

The 11-time DP World Tour winner's best finish on LIV was a tie for second in Virginia in June 2025.

"I've decided not to pursue LIV 2.0," said four-time Ryder Cup player McDowell.

"I'm grateful for the opportunity I've had over the last four years and want to thank everyone who has been part of that journey.

"I look forward to the next chapter in my career."

articles.title: England-Republic of Ireland Under-15 World Cup match abandoned over alleged racism
articles.text:
England walked off the pitch during a match at the Under-15 World Cup after an allegation of racism by a Republic of Ireland player, which resulted in the game being abandoned.

Following an altercation between players from both sides, shortly before the end of the match in Azerbaijan on Monday, an England player approached his bench and made a complaint to coaching staff.

Match footage then showed England staff members relaying the complaint to the referee, alleging a racist slur had been said, and calling their players off.

Republic of Ireland were leading 4-1 at the time of the incident.

World governing body Fifa told BBC Sport it is investigating and gathering reports.

"Fifa is aware of an incident at the U-15 World Cup and Festival match between England and the Republic of Ireland," a spokesperson said.

"The match was abandoned by the referee following England's refusal to continue.

"The official reports are being gathered, and the matter will be referred to the independent disciplinary committee, who will decide in due course."

The Football Association (FA) told BBC Sport it is awaiting more information and was in touch with Fifa, adding the wellbeing of players is a priority.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has also been contacted for comment.

articles.title: ATP doubles proposals: Players and legends sign open letter to prevent cuts
articles.text:
More than 150 men's doubles players - including British world number one Henry Patten and the legendary Bryan brothers - have urged the ATP Tour to rethink "drastic" changes which they believe could kill the format.

In a show of collective action, the players have written an open letter to the men's governing body as they fight proposals which would cut draw sizes and reduce prize money from 2028.

"We're at risk of losing a discipline of tennis which is historic - but has a big future," Dutch player Sem Verbeek, one of the architects of the letter, told BBC Sport.

"These proposals would destroy careers, livelihoods and dreams."

The ATP proposed halving the doubles draws at its flagship Masters 1000 events to 16 teams, with smaller tournaments reduced to eight teams.

The percentage of prize money devoted to doubles could fall from 20% to 10% - with the difference redistributed to singles players.

On Monday, a group of 137 current players, 28 legends and 20 national federations signed a letter which they hope will pressure the ATP into rethinking the proposals.

The tour's board - comprised of chairman Andrea Gaudenzi, four tournament representatives and four player representatives - will vote on the plans at next month's ATP Finals in Turin.

The doubles reform is part of a wider review by the ATP, which it says is designed to "strengthen" the tour from 2028.

The ATP aims to create "a more sustainable long-term model", insisting it wants to "maintain the important role" of doubles.

"Commercial success matters. Fairness, player welfare and the long-term health of tennis matter just as much," the players' letter says.

"Let us grow tennis together, without leaving doubles players behind."

The proposals provoked an angry response from the men's doubles cohort when they were revealed in July.

British pair Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash, who won Wimbledon in 2025 and became world number ones, accused the ATP of trying to "kill part of the sport".

Others within tennis believe reform is needed. They suggest a 20% share of the prize money for doubles is disproportionate to the interest shown by fans.

The doubles players argue the ATP should do more to promote their discipline and attract greater audiences, pointing out it is the format played by most club members and therefore more relatable.

The ATP says the proposals are based on data-led analysis centred on costs, revenue and viewership.

With fewer singles players now competing in doubles, it believes the current size of the standalone doubles events puts severe strain on tournaments.

"We support progress. We also understand the need to grow the sport, strengthen tournaments and increase commercial value," the players' letter says.

"Still, the proposed reforms go much too far."

articles.title: Jason Wilcox: Why is director of football in line of fire from Man Utd fans?
articles.text:
As the clock ticked down during Manchester United's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the home fans made it clear what they thought about director of football Jason Wilcox.

Singing his name along with an obscenity, the message was brutal and to the point. It was sung by a majority of the United supporters, and on more than one occasion.

It came less than two weeks after United defender Lisandro Martinez had launched a blistering attack on the club's hierarchy for not strengthening the squad, with a particular message for Wilcox.

"I expect more from our technical director," said Martinez.

Pressure is growing on United boss Michael Carrick after eight games without a win - their worst run since 2015-16 - and two three-goal defeats in a week.

But focus is turning to Wilcox too.

Wilcox is a former England winger who won the Premier League with Blackburn in 1994-95.

He joined United in April 2024 - initially as technical director after 15 months in a similar role at Manchester City, where he had previously been in charge of the academy.

At City he worked with current United chief executive Omar Berrada and also Stephen Torpey, who was appointed United's head of academy in August 2025.

When he arrived, it was said by United officials that Wilcox would work across all technical areas of the club to achieve "highest standards of performance" and would be answerable to the sporting director.

That changed the following December, when that sporting director - Dan Ashworth - was sacked amid a difference of opinion over who should replace Erik ten Hag as manager.

Ten months on, a poor series of results and dissatisfaction with transfer business has put Wilcox in the spotlight.

There are some who have sympathy with the position Wilcox finds himself in. The 55-year-old is not in charge of transfer budgets, which are set at a higher level.

Wilcox was also - obviously - not responsible for the injury Manuel Ugarte sustained playing for Uruguay at the World Cup, which wrecked a plan to sell the midfielder in the summer to bolster the transfer budget.

He, too, was powerless to prevent Barcelona backing out of a £26m deal to sign England forward Marcus Rashford.

Both issues affected the amount United could spend in the summer - both on transfer fees and wages.

Wilcox rarely speaks to the media, and a general lack of communication means we don't know why United decided to focus exclusively on strengthening their midfield in the summer, rather than bring in competition at left-back for Luke Shaw and striking support for Benjamin Sesko.

With both players injured, that looks like a major error.

The general consensus is Carrick has been sold badly short, and Wilcox's job title - and the fact he is often photographed with United's new signings and quoted in official press releases - means he is being blamed.

Since arriving at United from Southampton, Wilcox has twice been given very public backing by his bosses.

On the first occasion - around Ruben Amorim's recruitment as successor to Ten Hag - it was Ashworth who lost his job while Wilcox kept his.

Thirteen months later, when Amorim railed publicly against interference around United's formation - identifying Wilcox as one of those responsible - the Portuguese coach went, and Wilcox remained.

Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe is yet to offer his thoughts on the present crisis engulfing Old Trafford, but the United fans delivered their verdict loud and clear during the match against Bournemouth.

There are many reasons why United find themselves 16th in the Premier League and without a win in their past eight matches, but recruitment is one of the bigger ones - and for that, rightly or wrongly, Wilcox is getting the blame.

Since joining United, Wilcox has given one extensive interview - to the in-house Inside United podcast in October 2025.

A month before that, he spoke at the 40th anniversary gala dinner of United's past players' association.

But he rarely speaks to the media - there are only a couple of instances in the past 12 months of him stopping for the briefest of chats with journalists when he walked past an area they were waiting in to speak to a United player after a game.

After the defeat by Bournemouth, Carrick was asked directly if Wilcox and Berrada should speak directly to supporters.

"It's not for me to say who speaks and who doesn't speak, when they speak, and how they speak," said Carrick.

"I know my role here is to speak to you guys and represent the team and football club as best as I possibly can from this position."

There has never been an opportunity to ask Wilcox about the parameters of his role.

But with Carrick's situation as it is - his popularity intact and his status as a legendary figure at the club secure - the focus is moving to Wilcox.

United fans have made it clear they want him out - but does Ratcliffe feel the same?

articles.title: Sedgefield Racecourse fined after jockey taken to A&E in a horsebox
articles.text:
A racecourse has been fined £6,500 after a jockey was taken to hospital in a horsebox instead of an ambulance.

The incident took place in March at Sedgefield Racecourse in County Durham.

A disciplinary panel of the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) found that the racecourse had failed to comply with five "general instructions" within its Rules of Racing.

The injured jockey's identity was kept private but it was reported that he suffered a left clavicle and shoulder injury after a fall, and was examined by a doctor at the course.

He was cleared to race again but said he was still in pain, which resulted in a doctor advising him to go to A&E.

By then all the ambulance crews had left the venue, and he was taken in a horsebox with the medical staff following behind.

"The 'general instructions' require proper transfer to hospital with accompaniment from qualified medical staff not, as here, being followed in a car," the BHA panel said.

It also added that the jockey was in too much pain to get into the following car.

The other failings at the venue included a telephone line not working and "tired worn rooms not conveying a clean clinical area".

The racecourse has acknowledged the "errors and shortcomings" and an inspection took place in April which revealed "significant progress".

articles.title: Ballon d'Or predictions: Will Lamine Yamal, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe or Lionel Messi win?
articles.text:
The Ballon d'Or winner will be announced in London on 26 October - but who is going to win it?

Bookmakers have Spain winger Lamine Yamal and England captain Harry Kane very close together as clear favourites.

Lamine Yamal won La Liga with Barcelona and the World Cup with Spain, while Kane scored 73 goals for German champions Bayern Munich and England.

Eight-time winner Lionel Messi, of Argentina and Inter Miami, and Real Madrid's France forward Kylian Mbappe are the other probable candidates.

Or how about one of Paris St-Germain's back-to-back European champions?

BBC Sport asked several of its football experts who they think should take home the award.

European football expert Julien Laurens: I think he was the best player in Europe last season, especially in the Champions League where he was outstanding. He helped lead the team to another title, a back-to-back one.

He got the penalty in the final, scored in both semi-finals, in the quarter-final, and in the last 16. He was amazing in those huge, huge games where you want your best players to step up. He deserves to win the Ballon d'Or for being the best player in the world all the way up to the World Cup.

He won't win it, unfortunately, because Lamine Yamal, for the player he is and how entertaining and spectacular he is, didn't really shine at the World Cup, even if Spain won it. He didn't really do that well in the Champions League for Barcelona, getting knocked out early. However, his style of football means he'll probably win it - but it should be Kvaratskhelia.

Ex-Liverpool and Blackburn full-back Stephen Warnock: I think it will be Lamine Yamal for helping Spain to win the World Cup. If you were asking who else is in the hunt, I would say Michael Olise, but my pick personally would be Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, he is unbelievable. I love watching him play. He had such an impact for Paris St-Germain and last season he was incredible. I just don't think he will get the votes with Georgia not being in the World Cup.

BBC Radio 5 Live Euro Leagues guest and Athletic reporter Rory Smith: It will probably go to Lamine Yamal because it generally goes to someone who has won the biggest trophy, and this is the World Cup. It shouldn't be him because he wasn't necessarily Spain's most important player but his fame and talent means it will be him.

Personally I would give it to Kvaratskhelia. He has been the most exciting player in European club football for a while now, a valuable part of the PSG team who retained the Champions League, and crucially I think you shouldn't suffer because you come from a country who isn't in the running to win the World Cup.

Former England striker Ellen White: It's a tough one but I'll go with my heart - I'd love to see Harry Kane win it. I know he didn't win the World Cup but his numbers are absolutely extraordinary, with what he has achieved with Bayern Munich and England. Lamine Yamal had a few injuries but I know he won the World Cup and I'm sure he will win the Ballon d'Or one day. Michael Olise has also been phenomenal.

Norwegian football journalist Lars Sivertsen on Champions League Match of the Day: I would like to see Harry Kane win it, he deserves it. He is a real leader at Bayern Munich. He never makes trouble and is a role model. But I do wonder if him being a low-key character hurts him. The Ballon d'Or is a popularity contest. I love that he doesn't do all that but maybe he should.

articles.title: Women's Ballon d'Or 2026: Will anyone stop Alexia Putellas winning?
articles.text:
When the Ballon d'Or for best female footballer is dished out on Monday night, the chances are it will be a familiar figure that lifts the coveted trophy.

Spanish icons Aitana Bonmati and Alexia Putellas have hoovered up the past five awards - and Putellas is favourite to win it for a third time.

In May, the now London City Lionesses forward captained Barcelona to a quadruple, including a third Champions League trophy in four years and their seventh straight Liga F title.

Arguably, the only reason Bonmati is not in the running this time is because of a serious leg injury suffered on international duty in November 2025.

So will Putellas clean up once again? Is this trophy yet another example of Spain's increasing dominance of the women's game?

Or does anyone else on the 30-strong shortlist stand a chance of wrenching it from her grasp?

The reasons are obvious.

In Barcelona, Spain boast the world's most dominant club side.

The Catalans have contested seven of the past eight Champions League finals (winning four) and have been domestic champions every year since 2019-20, clinching the title by an average of 15 points above second place in that time.

Then, there is the national team. World champions in 2023, losing finalists at the Euros to England in 2025 and then winners of the Nations League last December, beating Germany in the final.

At the heart of all this success has been Putellas, who scored 21 goals and produced 13 assists during Barcelona's sensational season.

And it is not just her output that makes her case. Her all-round influence captaining an already stellar side cannot be overstated.

So, with 38 trophies in her possession already, the 2021 and 2022 Ballon d'Or winner appears poised to take it once again.

"Give it to her!" Spanish football expert Guillem Balague told BBC Sport. "Along with Marta, she is the best player in history. No doubt she was the best player in this campaign – and she won everything!"

Unsurprisingly, Spain have more players on the shortlist than any other nation (six) and eight of the starting line-up from the Champions League final are in the running for this award.

Among them are star striker Claudia Pina, who recently scored four against Real Madrid, goalkeeper Cata Coll and midfielder Patri Guijarro.

While Putellas is now tormenting Women's Super League defences in the blue of London City, it is another forward in this country that perhaps has the best case for consideration.

Khadija Shaw scored 21 goals in the league last season to fire Manchester City to their first title in a decade, adding another five in the FA Cup as they completed the double.

The Jamaica striker has been the WSL's top scorer for the past three seasons, scored 90 goals since her arrival in summer 2021 and was rewarded with a lucrative four-year deal in June.

"We haven't had a major tournament but there are some amazing players on the list," said former England international Ellen White. "I would love to see Shaw up there - brilliant goalscoring."

Shaw is part of a five-strong City contingent – they had none last season – but they all may fall short because they did not play in last season's Champions League.

Arsenal's Alessia Russo was second to Shaw for goals last season and impressed in the Champions League, picking up nine goals.

Last year, she came third in the Ballon d'Or voting last year behind Bonmati and club team-mate Mariona Caldentey.

That came off the back of the Gunners' Champions League victory in May 2025. Exiting in the semi-finals to Lyon this year may cost her a shot at winning the award this year.

One final candidate to break the Spanish stranglehold is, perhaps unsurprisingly, a Barcelona player. Poland's Ewa Pajor scored 11 goals in just 10 Champions League games last season, including a hat-trick in the final against Lyon.

The 29-year-old won the Women's Gerd Muller trophy for top scorer last season and finished eighth in the overall rankings.

Maybe it is her turn to take home the top prize.

The award covers the period from 3 August 2025 until 19 July 2026 and is based on individual performances, collective performances and fair play.

Selected international journalists – one from each nation in the top 50 of the Fifa world rankings - rank their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale.

The Ballon d'Or is then awarded to the player with the highest total number of points.

In previous seasons, the ceremony has come under fire for being too Euro-centric and for its scheduling during international breaks in the women's game.

This year, the event is taking place during the domestic calendar, solving the date issue. However, the lack of US-based players from the National Women's Super League (NWSL) remains a fair criticism.

One reason for this may be that the NWSL season runs from February to November and therefore does not marry with the dates this award covers.

It means the likes of Washington Spirit's Trinity Rodman are notable absentees from a list purported to chart the world's best players.

articles.title: Steve Borthwick and England's selection dilemmas amid World Cup countdown
articles.text:
With under a year to go until the 2027 Rugby World Cup, the countdown is on, with just nine competitive matches for the home nations until the tournament starts in Australia next October.

But while the World Cup spectre looms large, there is plenty to play for between now and then, starting with the resumption of the inaugural Nations Championship in November.

Steve Borthwick has named his 36-man training squad ahead of the Tests with Australia, Japan and New Zealand, and it gives a clear indication of the England head coach's thinking on both a long and short-term basis.

England play Australia on 8 November before facing Japan on 14 November and New Zealand on 21 November.

There is a recall for Joe Marchant, fellow centre Will Joseph is rewarded for his and Gloucester's excellent start to the season, while uncapped Archie McParland is the third scrum-half and uncapped Kepu Tuipulotu the third hooker.

On the whole, though, it is a tried and tested group.

"If we look at this training squad, it's not picked on form, is it?" former England wing Chris Ashton said on the Rugby Union Weekly podcast.

"It is a squad to get to the World Cup. Will Joseph is picked on form, but the vast majority is not. It is based on the experience and relationships [Borthwick] has with the players, and that is why Marchant is in there."

It is often the dilemma facing an England head coach. With 10 teams to pick from, there are always players playing well. How do you balance that with getting selection consistency from campaign to campaign?

Fin Baxter, Luke Cowan-Dickie, Jamie George, Will Stuart, George Furbank and Ben Curry - among others - have all been short of minutes or form this season. But they are all Borthwick regulars with priceless Test match experience.

"Part of the problem right now is that Steve feels he is under pressure to get results, so it is too late to make big changes," added Ashton.

"There just aren't many lads that have played much rugby."

The uncapped pair of McParland and Tuipulotu will both bring a freshness to camp.

But will McParland get much gametime ahead of the established duo of Jack van Poortvliet and Alex Mitchell, and will Tuipulotu get any minutes when competing with the highly experienced George and Cowan-Dickie?

"We know how talented Tuipulotu is, he is brilliant, but Nathan Jibulu at Sale has had two man-of-the-match performances and might feel slightly hard done by," said Ugo Monye, who also added that George Hendy at Northampton is another notable omission.

"In my opinion, we need to have a look at Hendy," he continued.

"He has been that good for that long. And if we are talking about form, where is [Bristol back rower] Fitz Harding?

"But I am sure Steve had a rough idea of his squad a month ago."

As ever, injuries will force Borthwick's hand.

Benhard Janse van Rensburg is out - a big blow to Borthwick given how he was fast-tracked into the set-up - while incumbent number 12 Seb Atkinson is on the rehab list, as is Exeter flyer Immanuel Feyi-Waboso. Their fitness will be monitored forensically by the England medical staff.

Meanwhile, the nailed-on starter at fly-half Fin Smith will also miss training this week with a calf niggle, although his injury is not thought to be serious. Charlie Atkinson was called up on Monday morning.

In the forwards, the selection picture is reasonably clear. Ellis Genge, George, Cowan-Dickie, Joe Heyes, Will Stuart, Ollie Chessum, Alex Coles, Maro Itoje, George Martin, Ben Earl, Tom Curry and Henry Pollock all make the 23 if fit.

Behind the scrum, especially at centre, it is more uncertain.

"I would struggle to answer [who will play in the midfield]," said Ashton.

Atkinson and Henry Slade started England's last Test, a crucial victory over Argentina in July, and could line up together again against the Wallabies on 8 November.

But Marchant and Joseph are also battling for the number 13 shirt, and a possible World Cup place.

"Marchant and Will Joseph are in a bit of a shoot-out," added Monye.

"They can both do a job on the wing and when you look at a World Cup squad you look at versatility.

"I would like to see bold decisions, but it is easy saying that when your job isn't on the line and you are trying to get selection right ahead of a World Cup.

"Will Joseph has been excellent and there will loads of fans who watch the Prem and will say against Australia, Seb Atkinson and Will Joseph are your ready-made 12 and 13.

"But I would be very surprised if that was to happen."

The players will be in camp until Tuesday evening before returning to their clubs for one more round of league action, before re-joining England next Sunday, seven days before the Australia showdown.

Borthwick has precious little time in camp with his squad before the Wallabies come to town, putting even more emphasis on established players, and established combinations.

Twelve months ago, England were in the midst of a winning run and started the autumn series full of confidence.

It is a different picture now after an underwhelming 2026, with just three wins from eight matches so far. As it stands, where the side will be come the World Cup in 12 months is anyone's guess.

England and Borthwick need a big November.

articles.title: Tadhg Furlong: Ireland prop cited for alleged groin grab on Gavin Coombes
articles.text:
Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong has been cited over an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster on Saturday.

Munster back row Gavin Coombes raised the allegation against an unnamed Leinster player with match referee Andrew Brace in the closing stages of the first half at the Aviva Stadium, but television match official (TMO) Colin Stanley could not find any video evidence at the time.

However, three-time British and Irish Lions tourist Furlong has now been cited over an act of foul play under Law 9.27, which says a "a player must not do anything that is against the spirit of good sportsmanship including but not limited to grabbing, twisting or squeezing the genitals".

A statement from the URC said "arrangements for the disciplinary process are currently in progress and will be announced in due course".

If found guilty of the offence, the 33-year-old would be in danger of missing Ireland's Nations Championship matches with Argentina, Fiji and South Africa in Dublin, as well as the finals weekend in London.

In October 2025, South Africa front-rower Jan-Hendrik Wessels received a nine-match suspension for grabbing Josh Murphy's genitals in the Bulls' URC win over Connacht.

For that incident, Wessels was handed a 12-week suspension - the shortest ban under World Rugby rules for such an offence - that was reduced by three weeks due to his "good conduct prior to and at the hearing and good record".

If similar action was taken against Furlong, he would potentially miss Leinster's Investec Champions Cup Pool match with Sale, as well as the festive inter-provincial derbies with Ulster and Munster.

Speaking after the 24-18 defeat at the Aviva Stadium, Munster head coach Clayton McMillan said he would "back our players 100% that if they make an allegation like that".

Leinster head coach Leo Cullen said he did not see the incident, which occurred in the 37th minute when Munster were leading, but acknowledged it was a "serious matter".

articles.title: Jermaine Pennant: Former Premier League winger needs more than 50 stitches after dog attack
articles.text:
Former Premier League footballer Jermaine Pennant says he needed more than 50 stitches after being mauled by a dog.

The 43-year-old was walking his two dogs in north London last week when he was attacked by a German Shepherd.

The former Liverpool and Stoke City winger said the dog latched on to his leg and refused to let go as he tried to protect his own dog, King.

King then intervened to help fight off the attacking dog, preventing "what could've been an horrendous situation", Pennant said in a post on Instagram., external

Pennant told the Sun, external he required more than 50 stitches to his right leg after sustaining four bite wounds in the attack and receiving hospital treatment.

He added that King was unhurt, but did not give details about the German Shepherd. He said he declined to report the attack to police.

"So I was attacked by a German Shepherd, I tried to protect King but the dog got my leg, I was on the floor with the dog still attached with no sign of letting go, until King intervened as he didn't know what was going on," said Pennant.

"But the minute he did he fought the dog off and saved what could've been a horrendous situation for me.

"King was unhurt with a little nip on his leg, but had blood all over him which wasn't mine. At this point I forgot the agony I was in, and my heart sank, but it wasn't King's."

The picture uploaded to Instagram shows Pennant with a bandage on his leg alongside King on a sofa, while he also thanked his partner Mimmi Montgomery for looking after them.

"My hero still protecting me and trying to look after me. King you're a legend, love you, man's best friend. Thanks Mimmi Montgomery for taking care of us both."

Pennant, who is a pundit for Talksport, made 231 Premier League appearances in a 19-year career before retiring in 2018.

At the age of 15, before making his professional debut, Pennant became the most expensive trainee in English football when he joined Arsenal from Notts County in a £2.5m deal.

articles.title: Brazil election: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn race around
articles.text:
A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics.

Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks.

At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers.

Led by Congressman André Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters.

Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics.

For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram.

The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.

Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".

"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.

On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.

The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.

In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".

Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.

Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.

Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."

By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.

Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.

"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."

In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.

"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.

She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."

Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.

In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.

"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

articles.title: Anthropic warns of AI's 'catastrophic risks' ahead of blockbuster share listing
articles.text:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.

Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.

"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.

Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.

The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.
